transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Yeah, um… I guess what brings me in is I keep getting stuck on how my face looks, mostly around my jaw. It looks kind of saggy and uneven to me, especially on one side.

It really hit me after looking at some family photos—funny, because everyone else was talking about how nice the day was, who blinked, all that stuff—but I just kept zooming in on my face. My wife says she barely notices anything, and clients don’t seem to react or anything, but I keep seeing it. It’s been bothering me enough that I thought maybe I should talk to someone.
How much has this concern about your jaw affected your daily life—like your work, relationships, or social activities?

It’s… not like I’ve stopped functioning, you know? I still go to work, I still meet with clients and do what I’m supposed to do. But I’ve noticed I’m slower getting out the door before client meetings, like I’ll get caught checking my face or trying to make sure the angle isn’t too bad.

And sometimes during appointments, I’m listening, but part of me is thinking about how my jaw looks from across the desk, which is embarrassing because that’s not what I should be focused on. I had a client the other day talking about retirement plans, and I remember thinking about the lighting in the conference room—anyway, yeah, it affects that.

Socially, I’ve skipped a few art openings. My wife likes those, and honestly I usually do too, but there are always photos, people posting things, and I just didn’t want to be seen or end up in pictures.
Have you been feeling down, hopeless, or losing interest in activities you usually enjoy, even aside from the concern about your jaw?

I’m not really sure how to separate it, honestly. Like, I still enjoy things when I’m actually there—well, sometimes. My wife and I used to go to these gallery openings, and there was this one artist who did these huge cityscape pieces, and I remember thinking the lighting in those places is always so harsh… which I guess isn’t really what you asked.

I don’t know if I’d say I’m hopeless. Down, maybe frustrated. But it feels tied up with the jaw thing, if that makes sense. I haven’t really noticed some totally separate sadness, but I also haven’t sat down and sorted it out like that.

Do you find yourself having the same troubling thoughts over and over about your jaw, or do certain things repeatedly because of those concerns, like checking your appearance or adjusting how you look?

Yeah… yes, I do. Before client meetings especially. I’ll go into the bathroom and check the mirror, then I’ll check my phone camera too, because somehow the mirror feels different from the camera—like one of them is lying, I guess.

And then I’ll mess with the lighting a little, or turn my head to see if one angle looks less… off. Sometimes I’ll change my collar or try to hold my face a certain way, which sounds ridiculous saying it out loud.

And it’s not just checking. I catch myself comparing my face to other people, like younger advisors at work, or people at those gallery events my wife likes. Someone will be talking and I’ll be looking at their jawline or thinking, “Why does mine look like that?” instead of actually staying in the conversation.
Has this concern about your jaw ever led you to avoid certain situations altogether, such as social events or even work-related activities, even beyond just skipping art openings?

Yeah, a little. I mean, I’m still going to work—I haven’t canceled client meetings or anything like that. Though I’ll admit I’m slower getting out the door before them, because I get stuck checking my face, and then I’m annoyed because I’m already thinking about it before I even get there.

And during appointments I can usually do my job, but sometimes I’m not as present as I should be. I’ll be listening, but also thinking about whether they’re noticing my jaw, or the lighting, or whatever.

The clearer avoidance has been social stuff, like the art openings. My wife likes going, and I do too, normally, but I’ve skipped a few because I didn’t want to be seen or photographed. There’s always someone taking pictures at those things now. So… work, not fully avoiding, but affected. Socially, yeah, I’ve avoided some.
When you're feeling most upset about your jaw, does it feel more like a sadness, an anxiety, or frustration that you're feeling?

I’m not sure it’s one clean thing. I want to say anxiety first, because it’s that kind of tight feeling, like I need to fix it before someone notices. But then if I’ve already left the house or I see a picture, it turns more into frustration.

Sadness… maybe a little, but not like sitting around crying. It’s more like being irritated with myself, if that makes sense. Like when you’re trying to get ready and the bathroom lighting is doing that weird overhead shadow thing—actually, we replaced those bulbs last year and I thought that would help, which sounds silly now. But yeah, I don’t know. Mostly anxious and frustrated, I think.

Have there been times when your concern about your jaw made you feel so self-conscious or anxious that it was hard to function normally, even in everyday situations like walking into a room, speaking up in a meeting, or talking to someone new?

Yeah… I mean, not like I can’t function at all. I do still get through my day, and I haven’t stopped working or anything.

But it does slow me down. Before client meetings I’ll get stuck checking, and then I’m late getting out the door—or not late exactly, but cutting it closer than I should. And then once I’m in the appointment, I can usually focus, but sometimes I’m only half there because part of me is thinking about how my face looks from that angle.

It’s funny, meetings have all these glass walls now, or reflective surfaces, and I’ll catch myself noticing that instead of listening for a second. Anyway… socially it’s been more obvious. I’ve skipped a few art openings with my wife because I didn’t want to be seen, or end up in someone’s photo. So yes, it’s made normal things harder, just not to the point where I’m completely unable to do them.
Can you recall if your concern about your jaw started before or after you began feeling down, frustrated, or losing interest in activities you usually enjoy?

I’m not totally sure how to separate those out. What I really remember is seeing myself in those family photos and getting stuck on this sagging, uneven look around my jaw and one side of my face. That’s the thing that kind of brought me in.

And then, you know, my wife will say she barely notices it, and clients haven’t said anything—if anything they probably aren’t looking that closely—but once I saw it, I couldn’t unsee it. So if I had to answer, the jaw concern feels like the main thing I noticed first, or at least the thing that started taking up space in my head. The feeling down or frustrated is more tied to getting stuck on it, I think.
Do you find yourself doing certain things over and over again—like checking your appearance, comparing yourself to others, or adjusting how you look—in response to your concern about your jaw?

Yeah, I do. Probably more than I like to admit.

Before client meetings especially, I’ll check the bathroom mirror, then I’ll open my phone camera and check again, sometimes a few times. And I’ll mess with the lighting, like if the overhead light is making it look worse—though I know that sounds ridiculous because office bathrooms all have terrible lighting anyway. I’ll adjust my collar or sort of turn my face to see if there’s a better angle.

And then out in the world I’ll catch myself comparing my face to other people’s, like younger advisors at work or people at gallery events. I’ll be in the middle of a conversation and part of my brain is looking at their jawline instead of listening, which is… not great.

Would you say your concern about your jaw causes you significant distress or makes it hard for you to function in important areas of your life, like work or relationships, beyond just occasional frustration?

Yeah, I’d say it’s more than just being annoyed with myself, unfortunately. I still do my job—I mean, clients aren’t leaving or anything—but it affects me.

Like before appointments, I can get slowed down checking how my jaw looks, and then I’m rushing out the door. And during some meetings I’m not fully there, which bothers me because that’s not really how I usually am professionally.

And with my wife, we used to go to more gallery things—she’s much better at that whole scene than I am, honestly, she can talk to anyone about a painting for twenty minutes—but I’ve skipped a few art openings because I didn’t want to be seen or end up in someone’s photo. So… yes, it’s not ruining everything, but it is getting in the way.
Do you feel that the way your jaw looks is a defect or something that makes you look abnormal, or is it more about aging and you just happen to notice it more now?

I guess… it feels like a defect, yeah, or at least like something off. The word “abnormal” sounds a little strong when I say it out loud, but that’s kind of what my brain does with it.

It’s that sagging, uneven look around my jaw, and one side of my face just seems different to me—especially after those family photos. Funny thing is, those photos were supposed to be nice, you know, everybody together, kids running around, someone always blinking in half the shots… but I just kept zooming in on my face.

My wife says she barely sees what I’m talking about, and clients don’t seem to notice anything. But I keep getting stuck on it anyway. Maybe aging is part of it, I don’t know, but it doesn’t feel like just “getting older” to me. It feels like something looks wrong.
